Laura Galante, a former director of the Cyber Threat Intelligence Integration Center, warns that Iran could retaliate against new US strikes with cyberattacks on American infrastructure, citing "good precedent" and encouraging operators to strengthen basic defenses as the risk grows.     Galante Warns Iran Could Target US Infrastructure
    Laura Galante, a former director of the Cyber Threat Intelligence Integration Center, warns that Iran could retaliate against new US strikes with cyberattacks on American infrastructure, citing "good precedent" and encouraging operators to strengthen basic defenses as the risk grows. Her comments come after reports that US and state officials believe Iranian hackers were likely behind attacks on more than 30 municipal water systems in Minnesota. At a Cabinet meeting Friday, President Trump rejected that explanation and blamed Minnesota's government for the attacks, without providing evidence. Galante speaks with Joe Mathieu and Kailey Leinz on the late edition of Bloomberg's "Balance of Power." (Source: Bloomberg)
    Miller Warns of 'Drastic Expansion' of Iran War
    Aaron David Miller, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, warns that a new US attack on Iran could trigger a "major and drastic" expansion of the conflict. His comments come amid reports that President Donald Trump has ordered a fresh round of strikes that could begin as soon as this weekend, as the US and Israel reportedly consider targeting Iranian energy infrastructure. Miller says a limited bombing campaign is unlikely to change Tehran's calculations, while renewed escalation would make progress toward a Gaza ceasefire even less likely. He speaks with Joe Mathieu and Kailey Leinz on the late edition of Bloomberg's "Balance of Power." (Source: Bloomberg)

The 24-year-old had persuaded a lot of people to give him a lot of money for a hedge fund, after previously working for OpenAI and the FTX Future Fund, a charitable arm of the fraudulent crypto empire of Sam Bankman-Fried, who is now in prison. Aschenbrenner ploughed that money into debt-fuelled bets on artificial intelligence companies, earning huge returns until he found out that stocks can also fall. The trader dubbed the “Nostradamus of AI” would have been hard-pressed to foresee how quickly his high-flying hedge fund would run into trouble. The firm’s rapid downward spiral is a familiar tale, as Silicon Valley and Wall Street once again threw their weight behind a bright-eyed but untested investor who promised this time would be different. “Everybody always wants to find the next golden child,” said one longtime hedge fund executive. “It just keeps happening.” In less than 24 hours — which included a conversation between Griffin and Aschenbrenner — Griffin’s Citadel hedge fund reached out to Situational Awareness and snapped up the investments at a discount, according to a person familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified citing private information. It was a startling reversal for Aschenbrenner, a former researcher at OpenAI who – before starting his hedge fund roughly two years ago — had no previous investment experience. Through it all, we had games. They always brought us back together.
